title: Dielectric
description: Electrically insulating substance able to be polarised by an applied electric field
wiki_lead:
In electromagnetism, a dielectric (or dielectric medium) is an electrical insulator that can be polarised by an applied electric field. When a dielectric material is placed in an electric field, electric charges do not flow through the material as they do in an electrical conductor, because they have no loosely bound, or free, electrons that may drift through the material, but instead they shift, only slightly, from their average equilibrium positions, causing dielectric polarisation. Because of dielectric polarisation, positive charges are displaced in the direction of the field and negative charges shift in the direction opposite to the field. This creates an internal electric field that reduces the overall field within the dielectric itself. If a dielectric is composed of weakly bonded molecules, those molecules not only become polarised, but also reorient so that their symmetry axes align to the field.
The study of dielectric properties concerns storage and dissipation of electric and magnetic energy in materials. Dielectrics are important for explaining various phenomena in electronics, optics, solid-state physics and cell biophysics.

In electromagnetism, a dielectric (or dielectric medium) is an electrical insulator that can be polarised by an applied electric field. When a dielectric material is placed in an electric field, electric charges do not flow through the material as they do in an electrical conductor, because they have no loosely bound, or free, electrons that may drift through the material, but instead they shift, only slightly, from their average equilibrium positions, causing dielectric polarisation. Because of dielectric polarisation, positive charges are displaced in the direction of the field and negative charges shift in the direction opposite to the field. This creates an internal electric field that reduces the overall field within the dielectric itself. If a dielectric is composed of weakly bonded molecules, those molecules not only become polarised, but also reorient so that their symmetry axes align to the field.
The study of dielectric properties concerns storage and dissipation of electric and magnetic energy in materials. Dielectrics are important for explaining various phenomena in electronics, optics, solid-state physics and cell biophysics.


Terminology
Although the term insulator implies low electrical conduction, dielectric typically means materials with a high polarizability. The latter is expressed by a number called the relative permittivity. Insulator is generally used to indicate electrical obstruction while dielectric is used to indicate the energy storing capacity of the material (by means of polarisation). A common example of a dielectric is the electrically insulating material between the metallic plates of a capacitor. The polarisation of the dielectric by the applied electric field increases the capacitor's surface charge for the given electric field strength.
The term dielectric was coined by William Whewell (from dia + electric) in response to a request from Michael Faraday.
A perfect dielectric is a material with zero electrical conductivity, thus exhibiting only a displacement current; therefore it stores and returns electrical energy as if it were an ideal capacitor.


Electric susceptibility

The electric susceptibility χe of a dielectric material is a measure of how easily it polarises in response to an electric field. This, in turn, determines the electric permittivity of the material and thus influences many other phenomena in that medium, from the capacitance of capacitors to the speed of light.
It is defined as the constant of proportionality (which may be a tensor) relating an electric field 𝐄 to the induced dielectric polarisation density 𝐏 such that
𝐏=ε0χe𝐄,
where ε0 is the electric permittivity of free space.
The susceptibility of a medium is related to its relative permittivity εr by
χe =εr−1.
So in the case of a classical vacuum,
χe =0.
The electric displacement 𝐃 is related to the polarisation density 𝐏 by
𝐃 = ε0𝐄+𝐏 = ε0(1+χe)𝐄 = ε0εr𝐄.


Dispersion and causality
In general, a material cannot polarise instantaneously in response to an applied field. The more general formulation as a function of time is
𝐏(t)=ε0∫−∞tχe(t−t′)𝐄(t′)dt′.
That is, the polarisation is a convolution of the electric field at previous times with time-dependent susceptibility given by χe(Δt). The upper limit of this integral can be extended to infinity as well if one defines χe(Δt)=0 for Δt<0. An instantaneous response corresponds to Dirac delta function susceptibility χe(Δt)=χeδ(Δt) .
It is more convenient in a linear system to take the Fourier transform and write this relationship as a function of frequency. Due to the convolution theorem, the integral becomes a simple product,
𝐏(ω)=ε0χe(ω)𝐄(ω).
The susceptibility (or equivalently the permittivity) is frequency dependent. The change of susceptibility with respect to frequency characterises the dispersion properties of the material.

grok_lead: A dielectric is an electrical insulator, or non-conducting material, that can become polarized in the presence of an applied electric field, resulting in the separation of positive and negative charges within the material to form electric dipoles. This polarization produces an internal electric field that partially opposes the applied field, thereby reducing the net electric field strength within the dielectric. Unlike conductors, dielectrics contain no free charges that allow significant current flow, making them ideal for storing electrostatic energy without dissipation. The key property characterizing a dielectric is its dielectric constant (also known as relative permittivity, denoted as Îº or Îµ_r), which is the ratio of the permittivity of the material to that of free space (vacuum) and is always greater than or equal to 1. For most materials, Îº exceeds 1, indicating enhanced ability to store electric charge compared to vacuum; for example, water has a dielectric constant of about 80 at room temperature, while dry air is approximately 1.0006. In practical applications, such as capacitors, inserting a dielectric between the plates increases the capacitance by a factor of Îº, allowing greater charge storage for a given voltage, as described by the relation C = Îº Îµ_0 A / d, where A is the plate area and d is the separation. Another important metric is the dielectric strength, the maximum electric field the material can withstand before electrical breakdown occurs and conduction begins. Dielectrics exhibit polarization through several microscopic mechanisms, including electronic polarization (displacement of electron clouds), ionic polarization (shift of ions in lattices), and orientational polarization (alignment of permanent dipoles in polar molecules). Materials are classified as non-polar (e.g., paraffin wax, with low Îº around 2â4) or polar (e.g., water or certain ceramics, with higher Îº), and some, like ferroelectrics, display spontaneous polarization and hysteresis useful in memory devices. The dielectric response can also be frequency-dependent, with losses occurring at certain frequencies due to relaxation processes, quantified by the imaginary part of the complex permittivity. Dielectrics play a crucial role in numerous technologies, including energy storage in capacitors for electronics and power systems, insulation in high-voltage transmission cables, and substrates in microelectronics and microwave devices. In modern applications, advanced dielectrics like high-Îº materials (e.g., hafnium oxide) enable smaller transistors in integrated circuits by reducing gate leakage, while polymer dielectrics such as polypropylene are used in high-energy-density capacitors for pulsed power systems. Ongoing research focuses on nanomaterials and composites to achieve higher dielectric constants and breakdown strengths for sustainable energy applications.
